hook: Conventional turbine blades melt at 2,200 degrees Fahrenheit, yet modern jet engines run even hotter.

sections.voiceover: Conventional turbine blades melt at 2,200 degrees Fahrenheit, yet modern jet engines run even hotter.
sections.visual_cue: Close-up of a glowing hot turbine blade in a darkened vacuum furnace.
sections.sfx_cue: Low industrial hum and the sound of gas rushing.
b_roll: Public domain footage of a vacuum casting furnace interior

sections.voiceover: Engineers solve this by using single-crystal nickel superalloy blades. How do these blades survive inside an F-22 Raptor?
sections.visual_cue: Microscopic view of a metal crystal structure transitioning to a clean, single-crystal view.
sections.sfx_cue: Mechanical clicking transitioning into a steady hum.
b_roll: Stock footage of an F-22 Raptor engine nozzle

sections.voiceover: But the real challenge is keeping the g' phase, a heat-resistant microstructure, stable at 1150 degrees Celsius.
sections.visual_cue: Graphic showing a temperature gauge hitting 1,150 degrees Celsius.

sections.voiceover: CMSX-4 castings also maintain this g' phase stability during the intense heat of engine operation.
sections.visual_cue: Bar chart comparing alloy strength retention at high temperatures.
b_roll: Technical chart showing g' phase percentage
Close up of a turbine blade casting

sections.voiceover: Researchers evaluated CMSX-4 castings on February 20, 2025, to confirm their extreme heat resistance.
